item.title: Cause of Antarctic ice gain identified
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-21
Cause of Antarctic ice gain identified While the Antarctic ice sheet has lost mass at an average rate of about 140.5 billion metric tons a year over the past two decades, satellite data showed a striking reversal from 2021 to 2023, when the ice sheet gained 695 billion tons — the largest increase on record. An international research team has now identified the mechanism behind the unusual gain, revealing a previously overlooked climate link between the tropics and the Antarctic ice sheet. The study, conducted by researchers from institutes in China, the United States, Japan, Belgium and Hungary, was published in the journal Nature on Wednesday. The researchers found that sustained warming in the tropical warm pool — a broad region where the western Pacific and eastern Indian oceans meet and sea surface temperatures are persistently high — sent large-scale atmospheric waves southward toward Antarctica. These waves carried unusually large amounts of moisture from the midlatitude Indian Ocean to Queen Mary Land and Wilkes Land in East Antarctica, resulting in persistent heavy snowfall. The researchers used several types of evidence, including satellite measurements of changes in Earth's gravity, records of snowfall preserved in Antarctic ice cores and computer simulations of atmospheric circulation. Wang Yunhe, first author of the study and an associate professor at the Institute of Oceanology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said such warming events in the tropical warm pool typically develop and persist for two to three years and occur roughly once in a decade. Similar, although smaller, fluctuations were observed around 2000, he said. The team also examined what caused the unusual warming and snowfall. Their analysis showed that human-induced climate change accounted for only about 9 percent of the increase in snowfall, indicating that the event was driven mainly by natural fluctuations within the climate system rather than by greenhouse gas warming. Wang, however, said the temporary increase in snowfall does not alter the Antarctic ice sheet's long-term trend. "The West Antarctic ice sheet is still losing ice, and some outlet glaciers in East Antarctica are also threatened by ocean-driven ice shelf melting and accelerated ice flow," he said. The findings help resolve a long-standing puzzle in Antarctic science: why the ice sheet's mass can fluctuate sharply over relatively short periods. "Scientists have tried to explain the unusual fluctuations in Antarctic ice sheet mass," Wang said. "Most researchers have focused on the central and eastern tropical Pacific and its connection with West Antarctica, where climate signals are strongest and easiest to detect. We looked at the other side — the western Pacific warm pool and its connection with East Antarctica — and identified a pathway that had not previously been recognized." In climate science, such a connection is known as a teleconnection, meaning that changes in one distant part of the climate system can influence weather and climate far away through atmospheric circulation. The study identifies a previously underappreciated link between the tropical warm pool and the East Antarctic ice sheet, Wang said. The finding provides a new framework for understanding short-term changes in Antarctic ice mass and could help guide future research into the climate of East Antarctica. limenghan@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Green energy fuels summer tourism
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-21
Green energy fuels summer tourism Heat waves drive up inbound trips helped by clean power SHANGHAI — French vlogger Yisa recently invited her parents to China for a summer trip, and they were all duly impressed by the cool and comfortable environment they encountered throughout their journey, even finding modern air-conditioning systems installed inside traditional yurts on the vast grasslands of North China's Inner Mongolia autonomous region. Like Yisa's family, who wanted to escape stifling heatwaves in Europe, an increasing number of foreign visitors are coming to China not only to explore its history and culture, but also to seek respite from high temperatures. The trend is giving rise to a new dimension of inbound tourism as visitors discover that China's "summer retreat" is supported not only by its diverse natural landscapes, but also by technological innovation, green energy infrastructure and an extensive transportation network. The phenomenon is also being witnessed in China's major cities. Vlogger Jenna Knapp from the United States recently visited Shanghai, where she sought refuge from 36.7 C summer heat in an indoor snow and ski resort. "If you know anything about Shanghai summers and you're looking to get away from the heat, this place is a dream," Knapp said in a video, adding that visitors could enjoy an artificial winter environment and ski rentals for less than $100. Her destination, Shanghai L+SNOW Indoor Skiing Theme Resort, is certified by Guinness World Records as the world's largest indoor ski facility. In subtropical Shanghai, where summer temperatures often exceed 30 C, the resort maintains an indoor temperature of around — 5 C across a 98,000-square-meter snow area, with a vertical drop of 60 meters. Behind such a cooling experience is an extensive effort to improve energy efficiency. The resort has adopted a range of energy-saving technologies, including solar power generation, an upgraded thermal insulation system, carbon dioxide refrigeration, waste heat recovery, ice thermal storage and dehumidification heating. Some 37,000 square meters of photovoltaic panels have been installed on the roof of the resort, reducing CO2 emissions by more than 2,000 metric tons annually, the resort said. The facility is more than a novel destination for summer visitors. It also showcases China's efforts to integrate energy-saving technologies with emerging forms of service consumption, while promoting the application of new thermal insulation materials, refrigeration equipment and other innovations. Yet the energy supporting such "chilling" experiences — from grassland yurts to indoor entertainment venues — comes from a much larger power network. "The 'air-conditioning freedom' stems from China's ultra-high-voltage power transmission networks and the rapid expansion of wind and photovoltaic power generation," said Cheng Haozhong, a distinguished professor at the School of Electrical Engineering of Shanghai Jiao Tong University. The cooling-off effects enjoyed by tourists in East China, Cheng said, are also supported by green electricity transmitted from the country's renewables-rich western regions. China's power supply has remained stable even during the peak summer season, when electricity demand has repeatedly reached record highs amid heavy air conditioning use. According to the 15th Five-Year Plan for the Construction of a New Power System, jointly released by the National Development and Reform Commission and the National Energy Administration on Aug 3, China's annual electricity consumption is expected to increase by about 600 billion kilowatt-hours during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30). To meet rising demand, China is building a diversified power supply system featuring coal, gas, nuclear power and renewable energy. The growth of green electricity is also helping cities meet rising summer demand, while advancing the country's energy transition. As of July 15, Shanghai had consumed more than 11 billion kWh of green electricity this year, about 25 percent more than its total consumption of green electricity last year and a record high for the fourth consecutive year. The combination of a stable power supply and growing green electricity consumption is helping provide the energy foundation for China's increasingly diverse summer tourism experiences. Beyond the power grid, China's extensive transportation network is making it easier for overseas visitors to reach cooler destinations across the country. While major cities remain popular with international travelers, more visitors are exploring summer destinations such as Southwest China's Tengchong, Yunnan province; Northwest China's Kashgar, Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region; North China's Qinhuangdao, Hebei province, attracted by their cooler climates and distinctive landscapes. The trend has been facilitated by China's expanding civil aviation network and high-speed railway system, which accounts for more than 70 percent of the world's total high-speed rail mileage. "This upgraded transportation network has turned the idea of having morning dim sum in a furnace-like city and enjoying the cool air at the foot of a snow-capped mountain in the afternoon into an everyday reality for travelers," said Cao Yixia, a research fellow at the Institute of Applied Economics of the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences. The growing popularity of China's summer destinations among overseas visitors is thus more than a seasonal tourism phenomenon. It offers an everyday perspective on the country's modernization — from green electricity and advanced infrastructure to convenient transportation and increasingly diverse forms of consumption. As more international travelers experience China's "summer retreat," they are gaining a closer and more tangible understanding of the country's development, helping foster more authentic and organic exchanges between China and the rest of the world, said Cao. XINHUA

item.title: China and Switzerland conclude trade negotiations
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-21
China and Switzerland conclude trade negotiations China and Switzerland have concluded negotiations to upgrade their free trade agreement, a move set to deepen bilateral economic ties and provide businesses with greater certainty amid rising global trade tensions, according to information released by the Ministry of Commerce. Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao and Swiss President Guy Parmelin jointly announced the completion of the negotiations in Bern on Thursday and signed a memorandum of understanding. The two sides began negotiations in September 2024 and, according to the Ministry of Commerce, after five rounds of talks, the upgraded agreement will provide a higher level of two-way opening-up in areas including trade in goods and services, investment and trade rules, creating new opportunities for bilateral economic and trade cooperation. China is ready to work with Switzerland to formally sign and implement the upgraded agreement as soon as possible and further strengthen bilateral economic and trade ties, the ministry statement read. Parmelin, who also heads Switzerland's Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research, described the agreement as an important milestone in bilateral relations which will provide a more stable, transparent and predictable institutional framework for long-term business development in both countries. Parmelin added that the agreement sends a positive signal of the two countries' commitment to openness, free trade and a rules-based international economic and trade environment. The China-Switzerland FTA was originally signed in July 2013 and took effect a year later. It was China's first free trade agreement with a country in continental Europe. According to the commerce ministry statement, following the conclusion of the negotiations, China and Switzerland will follow their relevant domestic procedures to enable the early signing of the upgrade protocol.

item.title: Enthusiasts flock to Xinjiang for celestial light show
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-21
Shooting stars: Astrophotographers flock to Xinjiang for celestial light show With its lack of light pollution and vast emptiness, the Gobi Desert proves a perfect spot to watch Perseid meteor shower Long after sunset, sweltering 40 C heat still hung over the vast, remote Gobi Desert as hot winds swept across the wilderness. Suddenly and fleetingly, a blazing fireball streaked across the star-studded sky, leaving a long, glowing trail and drawing loud whoops of amazement from stargazers. Astrophotographers stationed behind their tripods leaned forward to eagerly check their camera screens, hoping to have captured the fleeting moment. As the Perseid meteor shower peaked on Aug 12 and 13, observers and astrophotographers across China flocked to the Pterosaur-Yardang Dahaidao Scenic Area in Hami, Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, to witness the celestial event. "Stargazers are absolutely drawn to this place, and for good reason. Beyond minimal light pollution, the air here is extremely dry with little dust, creating exceptional atmospheric transparency," said veteran astrophotographer Liu Bing from Beijing. "As a result, stars retain their sharpness in camera shots, and less starlight is scattered away, making it possible to capture stunning pictures," Liu added. Astrophotographers can pair the varied, wind-eroded Yardang landforms with celestial subjects to create one-of-a-kind images. Liu and other astrophotographers recently attended the annual Sweet Whispers to the Galaxy Festival in Hami and captured images of the Perseid meteor shower. The event aimed to reinforce the area's reputation as a premier destination for stargazing. Many of them are from the China StarVision Alliance, a domestic platform for nearly 1,000 Chinese astrophotographers. Official data showed that Dahaidao registered about 25,000 visitor arrivals and more than 10,000 vehicles in early August. To cater to stargazers' needs, the site imposes strict nighttime lighting restrictions, and all stargazing spots feature 24-hour security patrols, emergency contacts and safety signs. For astrophotographers, advance preparation is vital, from understanding lunar phases to scouting locations with minimal light pollution. They check shooting sites in daylight and use apps to monitor weather and cloud cover, keeping close track of shifts in these conditions to the nearest hour. They also use apps to forecast how stars will move across the night sky and assess potential interference from the moon. "When observing the Perseid meteor shower, we need to locate the constellation Perseus and learn about the radiant point in advance — the spot in the sky from which all meteors seem to originate. As the radiant rises, it shapes the paths of meteor trails across the sky," said Wang Junfeng, a Beijing-based astrophotographer. "We often joke that we all became meteorologists just to take good photos." One night on the trip was mostly overcast, and the group waited patiently until clear breaks opened up between the clouds. "We could only seize those brief windows to observe the meteors and take photos," Wang said. Another member of the group, Liu Dapeng, set up three cameras at different locations before dusk, adjusted their shooting parameters and configured them to shoot a frame every few seconds until the predawn twilight. Liu said that smartphones, when mounted on a tripod, can capture the starry sky. Beginners can invest in cameras and wide-angle lenses based on their budgets, or opt for affordable secondhand gear. "After putting it into practice, they can think about whether they want to stick with astrophotography. It can be tiring, enduring outdoor hardships such as freezing cold and rain. "However, through astrophotography, I've made many friends across the country, and we enjoy shooting together. To me, the real reward is the joy of sharing tips and fun stories," Liu Dapeng said. "Safety is always paramount. It is very easy to get lost in the desert at night, so you should travel with others and take no risks. At night, you need to call out to one another regularly to check that everyone is safe," he added. Zhou Bo led a team to livestream the Perseid meteor shower from Dahaidao, Barkol Lake and Yiwu county across Hami. Drawing on his multidisciplinary knowledge, including geology and history, he promoted Hami's natural resources and cultural heritage while hosting the livestream. Zhou said he believes that the meteors stir curiosity and a thirst for knowledge among his viewers, fostering a desire for travel and inspiring wonder at the boundless cosmos. xulin@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Y-20 soars with national pride
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-21
Y-20 soars with national pride Decade-long service displays aircraft's versatility and durability The Y-20, nicknamed Kunpeng after a giant bird in Chinese mythology, is China's first domestically developed large military transport aircraft. It was officially commissioned in July 2016, marking a milestone in the strategic delivery capability of the People's Liberation Army Air Force. The project, led by the Aviation Industry Corporation of China's Xi'an Aircraft Industrial Group Co, began in 2007. Its prototype first flew in 2013 before entering service in 2016. With a maximum takeoff weight of 220 metric tons and a payload of 66 tons, Chinese pilots affectionately call it "Chubby Girl" for its wide fuselage. Ten years after its commissioning, the aircraft has not only deeply integrated itself into various combat readiness training sessions, but also displayed its power in non-military tasks such as disaster relief, humanitarian rescue and overseas transport missions. Over the decade, the aircraft itself has also evolved from a single transport platform into a family consisting of multiple variants including the original Y-20A, the Y-20B with domestically developed WS-20 engines, and the YY-20A aerial tanker. It has reached Asia, Africa, Europe and Oceania, building a channel for international exchanges and demonstrating the open, confident and pragmatic image of the Chinese military.

item.title: Ice, Chinese consumers' newest crush
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-21
Ice, Chinese consumers' newest crush Preference for cold drinks sparks debate on worth of traditional hot, warm beverages In China, drinking warm or hot water is a long-standing daily practice passed down through generations and believed to bring good health. However, fueled by an online buzz and changes to drinking habits, Chinese consumers — in particular social media-savvy young ones — are now putting ice, and plenty of it, in their drinks. At convenience stores, cups of ice have become a popular seller. At tea and coffee shops, "full ice, no water" has become a popular way to order a drink. Young consumers have also turned cups of ice into a social media sensation, using them to create DIY drinks that have attracted huge online attention. Gu Xiaoxiao, 36, a junior middle school teacher in Shanghai, is one of the ice drink devotees. For almost half the year, she has a cup of iced coffee at least once a day. "I usually start in April or May and keep drinking iced coffee until September or October. Besides my daily quota, I also order iced drinks when dining out or meeting friends. Recently, I even arranged to queue with friends for a popular ice cup coffee that had gone viral online," said Gu. According to a paper on China's urban consumer behavior in 2025, ice cup sales have grown by more than 300 percent for two consecutive years, with consumers in the first-tier cities of Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangdong province's Guangzhou and Shenzhen buying an average of 48 cups per person per year, reported ThePaper.cn. Publicly available data shows that ice cups are gaining wider market penetration, expanding from plain to flavored varieties and ice cubes designed for cocktails. A search for "ice cups" on Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, returned more than 40,000 posts. Zhang Yi, CEO and chief analyst at iiMedia Research, attributed the rising demand for ice cups to the past two summers being very hot and young people wanting to make their own drinks using ice cups. "The cold chain improvement has led to a cost reduction in ice transportation. On social media, the 'full ice, no water' trend has also become a new way for people to socialize," said Zhang. "Consumers are increasingly willing to pay for ice that is cleaner and comes in more distinctive shapes," he added.

item.title: Weather alert system taps tech, folklore
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-20
Weather alert system taps tech, folklore China offers world AI-powered MAZU as a meteorological safeguard solution "Mazu, protect our voyage on the deep," go the lyrics of a timeless Chinese folk song that is a plea to the sea goddess Mazu. "Safe journey out, safe return ashore." Embedded in this song is the soulful bond between local fisherfolk and the sea goddess who, legend has it, was born on the shores of Meizhou Island in Putian, Fujian province. Today, in the digital era, this ancient heritage has found a new, high-tech anchor. On the island, which has 30 kilometers of coastline and is home to over 1,000 fishing boats, locals no longer rely on prayers to weather storms. Instead, they find safety at their fingertips through a smart app that instantly decodes real-time winds, wave heights and tidal patterns. For Lin Haifang, a veteran mariner with a decade of island life under his belt, a simple app alert triggers his typhoon routine. He hauls up oyster shell strings, lashes down kelp rafts and steers his boat to shelter early. Even amid choppy seas and weak signals, the Beidou Navigation Satellite System beams alerts directly to his palm. "It feels as if Mazu puts the sea conditions right in my hand," he said of his early preparations, which keep his annual losses down and his income steady. Action plan proposed With the increasing frequency of extreme weather, the United Nations launched the Early Warnings for All initiative in 2022 to close gaps and protect everyone on the planet. China became the first to answer the call, proposing an action plan in 2024 and launching an intelligent meteorological early warning solution in 2025 named MAZU — an acronym denoting Multi-hazard Alert, Zero-gap and Universal. The system, deployed in seven countries, blends artificial intelligence forecasting models, data from Fengyun meteorological satellites, cloud computing and ground observations to deliver highly customized services. President Xi Jinping announced on July 17 that China will bring the AI-powered meteorological warning system MAZU to 30 countries over the next five years to safeguard homes around the world. He made the remarks while addressing the opening ceremony of the 2026 World AI Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance in Shanghai, calling for joint efforts to build a just and equitable global AI governance system. "All countries should take a people-centered approach and develop AI for the positive and for good. We should ensure that AI is an important driver for shared prosperity and common security," he said. Effective cooperation UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, who attended the meeting, praised the initiative, saying that the MAZU system could be one of the most important instruments for making international cooperation effective in protecting people and property. Zhang Xingying, director of the China Meteorological Administration's Department of International Cooperation, said the MAZU system is a perfect combination of fine traditional Chinese culture, AI and cutting-edge technology. "Naming the system after the Chinese goddess of marine weather reflects a unique touch of Chinese romance and demonstrates our cultural confidence," he said. In his view, Mazu's legendary helpers, the Thousand-Mile Eye and the All-Hearing Ear, are reflected in today's meteorological tools, with weather satellites and radar being the eye, and AI and physical models used to forecast climate disasters serving as the ear. "The core essence of the MAZU system goes beyond exporting China's early-warning capabilities," he said. "More important, it is about working with global partners to co-build a public safety solution for the long run." "This reflects the enduring spirit of the Chinese nation — centered on virtue, benevolence and profound love — which remains vibrant after thousands of years, and also highly aligns with President Xi's vision of building a community with a shared future for humanity," Zhang added. According to tradition, Mazu, the Chinese goddess of marine weather and maritime safety, was a Song Dynasty (960-1279) fisherwoman named Lin Mo, from Meizhou Island, who was later deified. Revered for her ability to predict weather, she died at age 28 during a mission to rescue fisherfolk from treacherous storms and was deified as Mazu, meaning benevolent mother. She is often portrayed as carrying a lantern to light the stormy seas, and was long credited with calming storms and guiding ships home. Belief in Mazu eventually was spread along maritime trade routes by Chinese seafarers and grew into a global bond, with over 11,000 temples and 300 million followers across 50 countries. During his tenure in Fujian, Xi actively promoted the protection of Meizhou Island and its unique Mazu culture. He planted trees on the island to protect its environment and allocated 2 million yuan ($297,500) to support the Mazu Square project to accommodate larger crowds, after he learned that the project's construction faced a tight budget. He said after a visit to the island that Mazu culture reflects the character of the Chinese nation, and its exchange and dissemination across the globe can help build a positive image of the Chinese people around the world. Spiritual asset Inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2009, Mazu culture now serves as a shared spiritual asset along the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road. As her golden statue travels for international processions and thousands of overseas people return to her birthplace each year, this ancient heritage remains a living bridge for global fellowship. Ke Li, deputy director of Putian University's Mazu Culture Research Institute, said, "The core spirit of Mazu culture aligns perfectly with the philosophy of the early-warning solutions, rooted in a shared commitment to putting people's safety first." The system also reflects Mazu's spirit of universal beneficence — echoing the goal of protection for everyone regardless of geography or background — and mirrors her ancient wisdom of foresight, blending traditional weather forecasting with modern rapid-response mechanisms, Ke said. Reflecting this spirit, the MAZU system has become a widely sought-after global public good. More than 40 national meteorological agencies are already using MAZU's cloud-based services, while customized versions of the system have been deployed in Pakistan, Djibouti, Ethiopia, Jordan, Mongolia, the Solomon Islands and Sri Lanka, according to the China Meteorological Administration. Nestled on one of the world's busiest maritime trade routes in East Africa, Djibouti has become a critical proving ground for the platform. An upgraded version of the MAZU system will be put into operation by the end of this year, which will sharpen its local forecast resolution from 9 km to 3 km. "MAZU 2.0 is very useful because we have several seaports on the coast," said Mohamed Ismail Nour, director-general of the Djibouti National Meteorological Agency, who expects to deepen port and shipping weather cooperation for safer maritime operations.

item.title: Deeper China-Africa media relations urged
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-20
Deeper China-Africa media relations urged African officials and media leaders called on Thursday for China-Africa media cooperation to move beyond equipment support and program exchanges toward coproduction and two-way storytelling, in order to help the African media better narrate their own stories and bring a wider African perspective to Chinese audiences. They made the remarks as the 7th Forum on China-Africa Media Cooperation opened in Beijing, bringing together about 400 government, media, diplomatic, business and academic representatives from China and 45 African countries. The three-day forum is being held as China and Africa mark 70 years of launching diplomatic relations in 2026 and observe the China-Africa Year of People-to-People Exchanges. Alhaji Mohamed Sarjoh Bah, the African Union's permanent representative to China, described the media as a strategic tool for development, cultural identity and economic opportunity, as well as a major force shaping international perception. He emphasized that Africa should not remain a passive recipient of information, and should instead become a producer and distributor of knowledge and ideas. He urged cooperation beyond content exchanges in film, broadcasting, animation, gaming and digital content to create value chains that generate employment and attract investment. Ahunna Eziakonwa, United Nations undersecretary-general and special adviser on Africa, made a video address to the forum in which she described storytelling as an essential tool for development. External narratives have long obscured African realities, but young African creators are changing that through streaming, animation and digital content, Eziakonwa said, adding that Sino-African joint productions, along with technologies adapted to African languages and contexts, could strengthen the continent's narrative sovereignty. Gregoire Ndjaka, director-general of the African Union of Broadcasting, underscored that cooperation between Africa and China should promote an exchange of stories, voices, ideas and experiences. Ndjaka noted Chinese support for African broadcasting and the provision of news, documentaries and other programs on AUBVision, the union's content-sharing platform, but emphasized that African content should receive greater exposure on Chinese platforms, giving Chinese audiences more opportunities to understand the continent from an African perspective. Evelyne Butoyi, communication and media minister of Burundi, which currently chairs the African Union, said Africa-China cooperation has improved grassroots access to information and cultural content. She cited the China-aided "Access to Satellite TV for 10,000 African Villages" project, which has provided transmission equipment to 500 villages in Burundi and extended digital television coverage in remote areas. Cao Shumin, deputy head of the Publicity Department of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and head of the National Radio and Television Administration, highlighted the scale of China-Africa media cooperation. Over the past two years, more than 80 Chinese productions have aired in Africa, while over 80 programs from 29 African countries have been shown on major Chinese television channels and streaming platforms, Cao said. The two sides have coproduced about 50 audiovisual programs, while China has organized 45 training programs for more than 1,000 media professionals from 32 African countries, she added. On Thursday, the forum also unveiled 80 practical cooperation projects and issued a joint declaration calling for deeper collaboration in content production, digital transformation and AI governance.
